claim: Kill switches for agent fleets are layered, not one global stop: (1) global stop -- pause all new runs across the agent/workflow, (2) tool-level stop -- disable one integration such as email sending, CRM writes, or payment actions, (3) escalation mode -- shift from autonomous to supervised execution requiring approval, (4) segment-level stop -- isolate to one customer, tenant, workflow, or environment. Authorization is explicit and per-workflow ('a named human who can pull the switch without committee theatre'), not a committee decision, and triggers should be 'measurable and boring' conditions -- approval-rejection-rate spikes, cost-per-run ceilings, duplicate-action detection, output validation failures -- rather than subjective judgment calls made in the moment.

claim: This source draws the sharpest distinction between agent kill switches and ordinary service shutdown: it explicitly rejects 'revoke its token and let it crash on the next call' and 'block its next tool invocation' as insufficient, because an agent mid-tool-call can still act before the next check. Instead a stop is execution-level -- 'the agent is stopped inside the process it is running in, before the next byte moves.' One click stops a single agent, another stops the entire fleet, propagating to every sidecar in under 100ms and reversible from the same console. Every activation is signed to an immutable audit log naming who pulled it and when -- the who-pulled-the-switch record needed for the postmortem.

read: Every activation is signed and written to an immutable audit log. So when the postmortem starts, you have exactly the evidence you need — who flipped the switch, when, on what, and what stopped happening 100ms later.

claim: The distinguishing operational problem named for agent fleets versus ordinary services: an agent that loops, calls the wrong tool, or hallucinates an answer can still return a 200 response within normal latency, so conventional APM reports a healthy system while agent quality silently degrades. Agent observability adds tool-call spans, online-eval scorers attached to live production traces, and per-span/trace-level cost rollups that generic uptime/latency monitoring does not provide. Like the UptimeRobot source (X-refmodel-rail-7-operations-005), this guide also declines to publish universal numeric alert thresholds, instead directing teams to convert production failures into eval cases and custom scorers -- corroborating that no industry-wide numeric standard exists yet for agent alerting.

claim: Current practice for agent-state DR treats four surfaces as at risk on a region failure: the inference provider's prompt-prefix/tool-schema cache, the worker's local scratch disk (plan-and-act traces, intermediate tool outputs -- kept local because it is faster and cheaper than durable storage per artifact), in-flight tool-call results that exist only inside an open inference call and are never persisted if the worker dies, and the partial plan trace embedded as unstructured text in prompt history with no structured record of what's done/next/decided. The prescribed durability unit is the tool call, not the session or run: a checkpoint is written before every tool call, capturing plan, prompt prefix, tool name, arguments, idempotency key and step ordinal. On failover the orchestrator does not default to auto-resuming a partially completed task -- it prefers fail-safe abort (mark the task aborted, surface a clear message to the user) over fail-forward replay, to avoid a second charge or a missed follow-up action. No numeric RPO/RTO target was stated in this source.
query: disaster recovery backup agent state checkpoint memory store 2026
read: Right before the agent invokes a tool, the orchestrator persists: the current plan, the prompt prefix, the tool name, the arguments, the idempotency key, and the step ordinal.
snippet: the unit of durability is the tool call, not the session

claim: A published maturity model does exist: the OWASP GenAI Security Project's 'State of Agentic AI Security and Governance' v2.01 (published 2026-06-01, covered here via a Cloud Security Alliance research note) defines five governance maturity levels 0-4: Level 0 'Unaware and Ad Hoc' (no formal recognition of agentic risk, informal minimal oversight); Level 1 'Experimentation without Guardrails' (pilots with no defined autonomy limits or escalation criteria); Level 2 'Policy-Defined and Human-in-the-Loop' (published governance policy, mandatory human review for high-impact decisions, a named accountable executive, established logging); Level 3 'Integrated and Continuous Oversight' (agentic AI treated as critical infrastructure with real-time anomaly detection, working kill switches, governance enforced as machine-readable policy); Level 4 'Adaptive and Self-Regulating Governance' (telemetry, red-team findings and regulatory inputs auto-tune guardrails, cryptographic agent identity). This is scoped to security/governance posture generally, not an operations-specific runbook standard: it does not define incident-response phases, alert thresholds, or DR practice -- those are covered in this batch only by practitioner blog sources (records 001-007), not by any standards body. Net finding for the fifth research question: a maturity model exists, but no published operations-specific runbook standard for agent platforms was found in this pass.
